title: Saying amin
hook: aloud or silently after the Fatiha, by school

segments.voice: Yesterday, hands in prayer, and your line: different hands. Did you catch someone doing a familiar thing in an unfamiliar way, and wonder who taught them? Day one thousand two hundred eight.

The imam reaches the end of the Fatiha in a loud prayer. The last line rings out, and in some mosques the whole hall answers with one long word, rolling from the front rows to the back like a wave hitting a wall: aameen. Visitors sometimes jump. In another mosque, same line, same imam's voice, and then nothing you can hear. Lips move, maybe. The hall is silent. Today, one word, and the ways it is said, or not said.
screen: `THE FATIHA ENDS.` → `A WAVE OF SOUND: AAMEEN.` → `ANOTHER HALL: SILENCE.`

segments.voice: First, where it comes. The Fatiha closes, in Pickthall's words, "Not the (path) of those who earn Thine anger nor of those who go astray." Right after that line, the word comes. Amin, a short request that Allah answer what was just asked. It isn't a verse of the Qur'an; it's the response to one. Next, why it matters. In a report in Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ says that when the imam says amin, the people should say it too, because whoever's amin falls together with the amin of the angels has past sins forgiven. So the word is small, and the promise around it is large. Then, the question the report doesn't settle: how loud? Shafi'i and Hanbali scholars teach that in the loud prayers, the imam and those behind him say it aloud. That's the wave. They point to reports of the Prophet raising his voice with it. Hanafi scholars teach saying it quietly, as a supplication, and supplication is best kept low, they say. Maliki teaching also keeps it quiet, with its own discussion of whether the imam says it in the loud prayers. Last, the Ja'fari school. Its jurists hold that amin is not part of the prayer, so it isn't said there at all. Shia worshippers pass straight from the Fatiha to the next surah. So one hall answers with a wave, another under the breath, and a third moves straight on to the next surah.
screen: `AMIN: ANSWER WHAT WAS ASKED.` · `WITH THE AMIN OF THE ANGELS.` · `ALOUD, OR UNDER THE BREATH?` · `THE JA'FARI SCHOOL: NOT SAID.`

segments.voice: The practice: notice it at the mosque, or notice it here. If you go to a mosque this week, listen for the end of the Fatiha and hear what your hall does. If you're at home, sit quietly and think of one thing you hope for today, something small and real. Hold it. Then just listen. Notice the difference between saying a hope out loud and keeping it under your breath. If you pray, you can say amin in the way your school teaches. The bell holds the time.
Saying amin. The response after the Fatiha: aloud in loud prayers for Shafi'is and Hanbalis, quietly for Hanafis and Malikis, not said in the Ja'fari school. Today's word.

Your line: aloud or silent. Today, when you agree with someone, notice whether you say it out loud or keep it to yourself, and what changes when you say it. Tomorrow, the small print of wudu. Day one thousand two hundred eight.

howItsDone: After the Fatiha, Shafi'i and Hanbali congregations say amin aloud in the loud prayers; Hanafis and Malikis say it quietly; in the Ja'fari school it is not said in the prayer.

fork.setup: you're visiting a Hanafi mosque, used to a hall that roars amin. the Fatiha ends and the room is silent. what do you do?
options: say it as you were taught, without making a scene.
fork.reveal: both ways are careful readings of the same reports. the Hanafi hall says it quietly; a visitor's amin is a difference, not an error.

original.note: Arabic: amin, said after the Fatiha, asking Allah to answer.

trapdoor: what you thought: amin is just how a prayer ends.
what it means: in salah it answers the Fatiha, and the schools differ on saying it aloud, quietly, or not at all.
what a scholar hears: the report of the angels' amin in al-Bukhari, jahr against israr, and the Ja'fari view that it is not part of the prayer.

School positions: Shafi'i and Hanbali aloud in loud prayers (imam and followers); Hanafi quietly; Maliki quietly, with internal discussion of the imam in loud prayers; Ja'fari not said (many Ja'fari jurists treat it as invalidating). Confirm each.
